papers.title_in_file: AutoQML: A Framework for Automated Quantum Machine Learning
papers.what_it_is: A framework that automates quantum machine learning pipeline construction and is benchmarked on four industrial use cases.

assertions.value: The authors report that AutoQML pipelines were competitive with manually constructed quantum pipelines on four industrial use cases.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VI Conclusion and Abstract, p.1 and p.8
quotes: Notably, the performance of the generated pipelines was competitive with that of manually constructed ones
demonstrating its ability to generate high-performing QML pipelines that are competitive with both classical ML models and manually crafted quantum solutions
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical benchmark on four use cases, Sec. IV, Fig. 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The manual pipelines were built by the authors for two of the four use cases, so the comparison is not independent.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical solutions were similar to the AutoQML solutions and that neither showed a clear advantage.
quotes: Overall, the classical solutions are similar to the AutoQML solutions, and neither demonstrates a clear advantage over the other.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark, Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results were produced with statevector simulations and that full pipeline optimization on current quantum hardware is infeasible due to financial and time constraints.
quotes: The results in this paper have been performed with statevector simulations.
a full pipeline optimization on current quantum hardware is currently infeasible due to both financial and time constraints
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own setup and limit, Sec. V.

assertions.value: The authors state that the framework in its current form is designed only for supervised machine learning problems.
quotes: the framework in its current form is only designed for supervised ML problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope, Sec. V.

papers.title_in_file: On Dequantization of Supervised Quantum Machine Learning via Random Fourier Features
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that bounds the risk gap between random Fourier feature models and quantum kernel or quantum neural network models.

assertions.value: The paper gives sufficient conditions under which random Fourier features reach a true risk comparable to quantum kernel and quantum neural network models, for regression and SVM classification.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V Conclusion and Props. III.3 to III.5, p.9
quotes: Specifically, our Props. III.3, III.4, III.5 provide conditions under which classical algorithms (i.e., RFF) could be comparable to QML models in terms of true risks.
Overall our results indicate two conditions for dequantizable quantum machine learning tasks namely alignment and concentration.
assertions.certainty_reason: Propositions III.3, III.4 and III.5, Sec. III.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study focuses on Hamiltonian encoding and that other encodings such as amplitude encoding fall outside the scope of the methods.
quotes: This study focuses on Hamiltonian encoding, a key ingredient to express QML models as finite Fourier series.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope, Sec. V.

assertions.value: The authors state that their ability to verify the conditions is limited by the computational cost of the Fourier transform.
quotes: our ability to verify these conditions is limited by the computational cost of the Fourier transform
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, Sec. V.

assertions.value: The authors report that on compressed high-energy physics data, simple sampling distributions for random Fourier features outperformed a quantum SVM.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V Conclusion and App. I, p.9
quotes: Using practical compressed datasets from high-energy physics, we numerically show that these simplified distributions can outperform QSVM.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical experiment on one dataset family, App. I.
assertions.reader_inference: The data are simulated proton-proton collisions, and the quantum SVM is a noiseless model.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Text Classifier - A Synchronistic Approach Towards Classical and Quantum Machine Learning
papers.what_it_is: A short implementation paper that builds a hybrid classical and quantum text classification pipeline in Qiskit and compares three quantum with three classical classifiers.

assertions.value: The authors describe a pipeline that keeps at most 20 TF-IDF features, reduces them by PCA to two, equal to the number of qubits, and trains quantum classifiers on an IBMQ simulator.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV Implementation and Results, pp.3-4
quotes: A maximum of 20 features are retained in the matrix.
PCA technique is used to further reduce the input features to two, which is equal to the number of qubits we would be using to execute the quantum algorithms.
to train the three Quantum Models using IBMQ simulator
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own experimental setup, Sec. IV.B and IV.D.

assertions.value: The authors state that the framework is optimized for three categories and two features, and attribute this to the limits of available NISQ computers.
quotes: The current QTC framework is optimized for three categories and two features
due to the limitations of available NISQ Quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope and limit, Sec. V Next Steps item 1.

assertions.value: The authors compare three classical and three quantum classifiers on a resume classification task and list the results in Figure 12.
quotes: The results are listed for comparison in Figure 12.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single small experiment; numbers only in Fig. 12 table, not in the quoted text.
assertions.reader_inference: Extracted text of Fig. 12 shows quantum accuracies near 0.81 and 0.57 against classical values near 0.85 to 0.90; table layout is garbled, so this is not verified.

papers.title_in_file: Practical limitations of quantum data propagation on noisy quantum processors
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that bounds the error in variational parameter propagation for quantum imaginary time evolution under gate noise.

assertions.value: The authors derive upper bounds on how the relative error in variational parameter propagation scales with the probability of noise, with an exact expression for partially depolarizing noise.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Theorems 1 and 2, Sec. IV
quotes: Specifically, we provide the upper bounds on how the relative error in variational parameters' propagation scales with the probability of noise in quantum hardware.
We also present an exact expression of how the relative error in variational parameter propagation scales with the probability of partially depolarizing noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational quantum imaginary time evolution will require single- and two-qubit gates with very low error probability to give reliable results.
quotes: such a quantum algorithm or the family of quantum algorithms will require single- and two-qubit gates with very low error probability to produce reliable results
assertions.certainty_reason: Consequence the authors draw from the bounds; the bound is proved but the practical conclusion is their reading.

assertions.value: The authors state that the bounds cover a single iteration under global Markovian noise.
quotes: In this work we presented upper bounds on the error incurred during a single iteration of quantum imaginary time evolution in the presence of global Markovian noise in the quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope, Sec. V.

assertions.value: The authors state that the amount of error suppression from probabilistic error cancellation, with respect to its overhead, is left for future work.
quotes: Exact details on the amount of error suppression with respect to the overhead needed for PEC are left for a future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, Sec. V.

papers.title_in_file: Path Matters: Industrial Data Meet Quantum Optimization
papers.what_it_is: A benchmark of QUBO formulations on quantum annealing (D-Wave) and linear-ramp QAOA (IBM) for an industrial press shop work allocation problem.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum annealing on D-Wave hardware consistently gave near-optimal solutions while linear-ramp QAOA on IBM devices struggled to reach comparable performance.
quotes: Our results show that QA on D-Wave hardware consistently produces near-optimal solutions, whereas LR-QAOA on IBM quantum devices struggles to reach comparable performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical benchmark on one industrial problem, Sec. VI.
assertions.reader_inference: The result holds for the tested modest problem sizes only.

assertions.value: The authors report that on IBM machines linear-ramp QAOA lags behind the classical simulated annealing baseline.
quotes: However, when deployed on IBM machines, it lags behind the classical baseline of simulated annealing
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result, Sec. VI and VII.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark uses a real industrial production planning problem, the optimization of work allocation in a press shop producing vehicle parts.
quotes: the optimization of work allocation in a press shop producing vehicle parts
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own setup, Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that even modest-size problems need significant quantum resources on all algorithms and platforms they tested, with noisy hardware and incomplete connectivity as main limiting factors.
quotes: Even modest-size problems require significant quantum resources to work for all algorithms and platforms we tested.
Noisy quantum hardware and incomplete connectivity seem to be the main limiting factors for scaling quantum computers to industry-level needs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' reading of their benchmark; the second sentence is hedged with 'seem'.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-Inspired Machine Learning for Molecular Docking
papers.what_it_is: A Huawei paper that combines a quantum-inspired classical Ising solver with a diffusion-model scoring function for blind molecular docking.

assertions.value: The authors report that their method, QDMD, reaches a docking success rate of 32.43% with 10 primed samples and 35.26% with 40 primed samples, and improves overall success by 2 percentage points over DiffDock under comparable time.
quotes: QDMD achieves a docking success rate of 32.43% with 10 primed samples and reaches 35.26% with 40 primed samples.
It achieves an improvement of 2 percentage points in the overall docking success rate, while operating under comparable time conditions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one test set, Sec. IV.
assertions.reader_inference: The gain is small and the quoted text reports no confidence intervals.

assertions.value: The authors report that on newer ligand structures QDMD improves by nearly 6 percentage points over DiffDock in cases where the RMSD is less than 1.
quotes: QDMD exhibits an improvement of nearly 6 percentage points compared to DiffDock in cases where the RMSD is less than 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one curated test set, Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors describe the quantum-inspired algorithm they use as a classical algorithm that solves Ising problems on classical hardware.
quotes: is a classical algorithm solving Ising problem on the classical hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own setup, Sec. II.C.

assertions.value: The authors state that the test set holds 363 protein-ligand complexes from PDBbind, randomly selected from those released after 2019.
quotes: 363 pairs of protein-ligand complexes from this dataset after 2019 were randomly selected as a test set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own setup, Sec. IV.

papers.title_in_file: Modeling Quantum Machine Learning for Genomic Data Analysis
papers.what_it_is: A Qiskit simulation study that compares QSVM, Pegasos-QSVC, VQC and QNN with three feature maps on binary genome sequence classification.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiments use the Qiskit AerSimulator with four qubits on a genomic benchmark dataset of 100,000 sequences in two classes.
quotes: we utilize the Qiskit AerSimulator, which replicates the properties and behavior of real-world IBM quantum computers
four qubits are utilized to handle the benchmark genome sequence dataset democoding vs. intergenomic [34] which contains 100,000 genome sequences with two classes of transcripts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own setup, Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors report that QSVM with the ZFeatureMap reached 51.89% training and 51.30% test accuracy, and that QNN reached its highest training accuracy of 54.38% with 51.65% test accuracy.
quotes: the QSVM algorithm achieves 51.89% training accuracy and 51.30% test accuracy
QNN achieves the highest training accuracy (54.38%) and decent test accuracy (51.65%)
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated results on a subset of one dataset, Table I.
assertions.reader_inference: For a binary task these accuracies are close to 50%, so the data do not show a useful classifier; the paper still concludes that QML enhances performance.

assertions.value: The authors state that their initial analysis indicates QML enhances genomic classification performance and that larger datasets are needed for deeper insight.
quotes: Our initial analysis indicates that QML enhances genomic classification performance.
Further studies with larger datasets will offer deeper insights
assertions.certainty_reason: Author conclusion; no classical baseline appears in the quoted results.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported accuracies near 50% do not support the claim without a classical baseline.
